metadata.title: eMobility Residuality Stress Test
metadata.description: Explore how the eMobility service would need to change when drivers, fleets, regulation, pricing, public behavior, or the physical charging network behave differently from today's assumptions.
metadata.naiveArchitecture: A registered driver presents an RFID key fob at a charge point. The charger calls a cloud authorization API, which reads the membership record from a database and either permits or denies the charging session.
metadata.residualArchitecture: Instead of treating one membership key fob as the only way to start and pay for charging, the adapted design separates four decisions: who or what may start a session, whether charging can begin, how the price is calculated, and who pays. RFID, vehicle recognition, fleet accounts, roaming, and walk-up payment can therefore change independently. Operational evidence and capacity controls help the network respond to regulation, new customer groups, and physical disruption.
metadata.note: This flagship dataset adapts the EV-charger worked example to the existing eMobility Productscape objects. It is a teaching dataset, not a claim that every residue has been implemented in a production system.

source.title: Residues: Time, Change, and Uncertainty in Software Architecture
source.author: Barry M. O'Reilly

stressors.name: A driver's key fob breaks at the charger
stressors.detection: Authorization-failure events, repeated tap attempts, roadside-support calls, and charger-panel telemetry.
stressors.attractor: A driver with little remaining battery is stranded at a functioning charger because the subscription credential—not the ability to pay or charge—has failed.
stressors.businessReaction: Let the driver charge without the original membership credential, identify the vehicle or accept another authorization method, and recover payment afterwards.
stressors.residue: Decouple charging permission from membership identity. Session orchestration accepts an authorization token from RFID, vehicle recognition, support, or walk-up payment, while billing resolves the payer separately.

impacts.effect: Makes seamless and predictable public charging depend on credential-independent recovery, not only normal authentication success.
Extends reliable charging to the moment when the driver's normal credential is unavailable.
Turns authentication from one RFID path into a recoverable choice of authorization paths.
Session success must include recovery starts, not only first-attempt RFID authorization.
Needs a visible recovery flow and a post-session path for confirming identity and payment.
Must validate multiple authorization token types without treating a membership record as the charging command.
Must start and track a session from an authorization token whose payer may be resolved later.
Must support post-session payment recovery and later association of the charge with a payer.
Owns the credential-independent authorization policy and recovery experience.
Owns a charge-start contract that remains stable while authorization methods change.
Owns delayed payer resolution, post-paid collection, and auditability of the recovered session.
Keeps charger discovery and session start recoverable when the driver's normal credential fails.
Makes credential-independent roadside recovery a benchmark for broad public-charging access.

stressors.name: A fleet wants one account for many drivers and vehicles
stressors.detection: Enterprise sales requests, fleet RFPs, account-onboarding workshops, and invoice consolidation requests.
stressors.attractor: The economically important customer is an organization with a single commercial relationship, while many drivers, vehicles, credentials, cost centers, and reimbursement rules use it.
stressors.businessReaction: Sell and operate a hierarchical fleet account with delegated access, consolidated billing, vehicle and driver assignment, and policy controls.
stressors.residue: Separate payer, account, driver, vehicle, and credential. Allow many authorization identities to resolve to one contract while preserving per-driver and per-vehicle usage records.

impacts.effect: Makes enterprise-scale electrification depend on a multi-actor account model rather than a consumer account reused many times.
Adds organization-wide identity, policy, and cost allocation to the fleet-cost job.
Changes access issuance into a lifecycle for drivers, vehicles, roles, credentials, and exceptions.
Becomes a scale test for the account hierarchy and assignment model, not only a sales volume measure.
Requires account hierarchy, delegated administration, policy, allocation, and consolidated billing as core product behavior.
Becomes the explicit model for fleet, vehicle, driver, assignment, and charging-policy relationships.
Must model the contracting organization separately from members and charging credentials.
Must support delegated fleet roles and scoped permissions rather than a single account owner.
Must consolidate usage while retaining vehicle, driver, tax, and cost-center detail.
Owns the cross-brick enterprise account model and its end-to-end behavior.
Owns delegation and permission boundaries for fleet administrators and drivers.
Raises enterprise fleet and workplace account depth as a competitive benchmark, not an optional consumer-account extension.
Carries fleet hierarchy, delegated access, vehicle assignment, policy, and exceptions into daily charging behavior.

stressors.name: Emergency vehicles need priority access to constrained charging capacity
stressors.detection: Health-authority procurement, emergency-service operating exercises, site-capacity alerts, and priority-access requests.
stressors.attractor: Charging is no longer first-come first-served: public-service vehicles must receive time-critical capacity while ordinary drivers and fleets are already using the site.
stressors.businessReaction: Offer governed priority contracts, reserve capacity, explain displaced sessions, and preserve a clear audit trail for every override.
stressors.residue: Introduce a policy-driven priority token into authorization and smart charging. Session orchestration requests capacity by service class, while site constraints remain separate from customer identity.

impacts.effect: Expands network reliability from average availability to differentiated service continuity for critical customers.
Adds governed capacity prioritization to operating a pan-European network.
Optimization must honor service priority as well as grid cost and site constraints.
Peak utilization needs a companion view of protected capacity and priority-service fulfillment.
Needs contract-driven capacity reservation, operator controls, and explainable overrides.
Must allocate power using service priority without embedding customer-specific rules in the optimization engine.
Must expose reservable and interruptible site capacity as explicit constraints.
Must attach a verified service-class claim to the authorization token.
Must coordinate priority, displacement, notification, and recovery across active sessions.
Owns policy-safe allocation behavior and the service-level evidence for priority capacity.
Owns the session state transitions when ordinary capacity is displaced or reserved.
Allocates constrained site power across ordinary and protected service classes with explainable outcomes.
Makes governed fleet and public-service capacity controls an enterprise charging benchmark.

stressors.name: Vehicles collide with charge points
stressors.detection: Sudden telemetry loss, impact or tilt sensors, camera events, site reports, insurance claims, and unusual support contacts.
stressors.attractor: Physical assets fail unpredictably, a site loses capacity, queues move elsewhere, and operators need evidence before repair, safety, and liability decisions can proceed.
stressors.businessReaction: Isolate the unsafe asset, redirect drivers, use spare network capacity, dispatch repair, and retain reliable incident evidence.
stressors.residue: Treat physical capacity and evidence as explicit parts of network operation: health events remove assets from availability, location publishing redirects demand, spare capacity absorbs loss, and camera or site evidence is attached to the incident.

impacts.effect: Makes physical damage detection and capacity substitution part of reliable network operation.
Extends uptime work from software incidents to damaged field assets and redirected demand.
Must distinguish unsafe, isolated, degraded, and substituted physical capacity.
Begins at reliable damage detection and includes evidence collection, dispatch, and safe recommissioning.
Needs physical-asset incident state, evidence, isolation, repair, and capacity-degradation views.
Correlates missing telemetry, site signals, reports, and evidence into a physical-asset incident.
Must carry safe isolation, repair, replacement, and recommissioning states for each charge point.
Must rapidly remove unsafe capacity and direct drivers toward viable alternatives.
Owns detection, triage, evidence linkage, and operational response across software and physical signals.
Owns the asset lifecycle from isolation through safe recommissioning.
Network reliability includes physical safety, lost capacity, evidence, repair, and demand redirection.
Coordinates detection, isolation, repair, alternative capacity, and safe recommissioning of damaged assets.
Makes rapid physical-site incident recovery a high-utilization public fast-charging benchmark.

stressors.name: Drivers leave vehicles at chargers for hours after charging
stressors.detection: Connector-state telemetry, completed-energy sessions that remain occupied, queue complaints, and falling site throughput.
stressors.attractor: The scarce product is parking time rather than electricity: technically available chargers remain unusable, queues grow, and subscribers cannot access promised capacity.
stressors.businessReaction: Make extended occupancy progressively expensive, warn drivers before penalties begin, and show the full rule before a session starts.
stressors.residue: Separate energy rating from occupancy rating. Tariff policy can apply a sliding time charge after completion, while notifications and receipts explain every transition.

impacts.effect: Makes predictable charging depend on fair access to occupied infrastructure as well as charger discovery.
Adds post-charge vehicle removal and transparent occupancy pricing to the end-to-end charging job.
The receipt and live session view must separate energy cost from occupancy cost.
Becomes an actionable measure of blocked capacity, not simply time without energy transfer.
Measures whether occupancy policy converts installed capacity into completed customer sessions.
Needs pre-session disclosure, countdowns, notifications, and explainable occupancy charges.
Needs operator policy, site exceptions, occupancy analytics, and dispute evidence.
Must model time-based occupancy tiers independently from the energy tariff.
Must rate energy and occupancy intervals as separately explainable ledger lines.
Must invoice, collect, refund, and settle occupancy charges with a complete audit trail.
Owns transparent disclosure and timely nudges before occupancy charges escalate.
Owns portable tariff semantics across direct and roaming sessions.
Explains energy and occupancy pricing before, during, and after the session.
Makes transparent idle-fee policy and notification a large-network customer-experience benchmark.

stressors.name: Petrol vehicles intentionally block EV chargers
stressors.detection: Camera or site reports, a recognized non-EV plate, occupied-bay signals without a charging session, and clustered driver complaints.
stressors.attractor: Charging bays become a target for deliberate obstruction; capacity is socially contested even though the charging technology remains healthy.
stressors.businessReaction: Identify and document the obstruction, apply enforceable occupancy consequences, redirect affected drivers, and make repeated blocking unattractive.
stressors.residue: No new architectural change is needed: vehicle recognition and incident evidence, spare-capacity redirection, and sliding occupancy billing combine to absorb the new behavior.

impacts.effect: Shows that reliable operation includes adversarial social use of the physical network, not only equipment health.
Treats blocked but functional bays as unavailable capacity that needs detection and redirection.
Must distinguish genuinely idle capacity from physically blocked capacity.
Reuses existing evidence, capacity, and pricing controls without introducing an ICE-specific subsystem.
Correlates bay occupancy without a charging session into an actionable obstruction event.
Removes blocked capacity from availability and redirects drivers.
Reuses occupancy policy instead of adding behavior-specific billing logic.
Coordinates evidence, site response, and capacity redirection through existing incident operations.
Reliable network capacity includes detecting and resolving deliberate obstruction of healthy assets.
Reuses incident evidence, capacity state, redirection, and site response for socially blocked bays.
Makes obstruction-aware site operations a benchmark for widely distributed charging networks.

stressors.name: Regulation mandates ad-hoc card payment at every public charger
stressors.detection: Regulatory monitoring, legal counsel, standards forums, public procurement rules, and competitors shipping compliant payment flows.
stressors.attractor: A driver without a subscription or roaming contract expects immediate, transparent point-of-use payment; membership can no longer be the only route to a charge.
stressors.businessReaction: Accept walk-up card payment, disclose the price before authorization, preserve existing subscriptions, and produce compliant receipts and settlement records.
stressors.residue: No fundamental redesign is needed: the charge command already accepts authorization independently from membership, so card payment supplies another token and billing path behind the same session contract.

impacts.effect: Makes seamless charging explicitly inclusive of drivers without an existing account or roaming agreement.
Adds walk-up price acceptance and card authorization to reliable public charging.
Accepts payment authorization as a valid charge-start token without first creating a membership.
Requires pre-authorization price disclosure and a receipt for an unregistered payer.
Must include successful walk-up sessions and distinguish payment decline from charger failure.
Needs an account-free payment journey that coexists with app and RFID experiences.
Must distinguish direct ad-hoc payment from roaming authorization and settlement.
Accepts a payment authorization token without coupling it to a member identity.
Keeps the session start contract stable across card, RFID, app, and roaming channels.
Adds card capture, receipt, refund, reconciliation, and payment-service-provider settlement.
Owns the channel-neutral authorization contract rather than a membership-only gate.
Owns compliant card collection and its separation from roaming settlement.
Makes walk-up access at a large energy-backed network a parity benchmark for the driver experience.
Provides account-free price disclosure, card authorization, receipt, refund, and payment support.

stressors.name: A major competitor cuts public-charging prices below our subscriber tariff
stressors.detection: Competitor tariff pages, driver-app price comparisons, partner notices, churn interviews, and a sudden shift in route-level demand.
stressors.attractor: Price becomes the visible acquisition benchmark; subscription lock-in no longer justifies friction, and operators must protect utilization and margin at the same time.
stressors.businessReaction: Respond by segment and context rather than copying one headline price: launch bounded offers, show total cost clearly, reward flexible demand, and protect unit economics.
stressors.residue: Decouple offer policy from metering, settlement, and session orchestration. Versioned tariffs and eligibility rules can change rapidly, while analytics measures margin, conversion, utilization, and competitor response.

impacts.effect: Tests whether the most reliable platform can also preserve operator profitability during price-led competition.
Adds transparent, competitive total cost to the promise of seamless and predictable charging.
Becomes the guardrail that prevents a price response from buying utilization with structurally unprofitable sessions.
Must show whether displayed savings and final billed prices remain trustworthy during rapid offer changes.
Needs segment-aware offers and clear comparison of subscription, roaming, and walk-up prices.
Needs operator controls for bounded campaigns, site eligibility, and margin-aware rollout.
Must version price policy and eligibility independently from ledger and session behavior.
Must connect competitor movement to conversion, utilization, margin, churn, and site-level response.
Must apply rapidly changing offers deterministically and preserve the policy version used for every charge.
Owns fast tariff response with explicit commercial guardrails and cross-channel semantics.
Owns the analytical feedback that distinguishes healthy price response from margin leakage or measurement error.
Provides the enterprise software and network benchmark against which price and bundled value are compared.
Provides a fast-charging utilization and customer-account benchmark for the North American response.
Tests whether a challenger combining hardware, network operation, and services can sustain a different price bundle.
Reliable charging includes choosing an offer whose displayed total cost remains competitive and trustworthy.
Shows the active offer, eligibility, comparison, billed price, and savings consistently through payment.
Connects competitive offer design to clear driver choice, deterministic rating, receipt, and margin evidence.
